items.issuing_body: U.S. House Committee on House Administration (Chairman Bryan Steil, WI-01)
items.title: House Administration Chairman Steil introduces the Stop Lawmakers from Predicting Act, barring members of Congress and their families from political/policy wagers on prediction markets
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, U.S. Representative Bryan Steil (WI-01), Chairman of the Committee on House Administration, introduced the Stop Lawmakers from Predicting Act. According to the Committee's press release, the bill would prohibit Members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from using prediction markets to wager on a specific government policy, government action, or political outcome, while continuing to permit wagers on unrelated events such as sports. Under the bill, violators would pay a fee equal to $2,000 or ten percent of the value of the prohibited transaction (whichever is greater), plus the net gain realized from the transaction; Members could not use their Members' Representational Allowance, Senate personnel and office expense account, or political contributions or donations to pay the fine; and Members who resign or retire without paying the fine could be referred to the Department of Justice for civil enforcement. The Committee states the measure builds on the Stop Insider Trading Act, which the Committee advanced on January 14, 2026. The bill must still pass committee and a floor vote to become law.
items.source_label: U.S. House Committee on House Administration — Press Release (June 18, 2026)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms (e.g., Kalshi, Polymarket), event-contract operators, government-affairs and compliance teams

items.issuing_body: U.S. Senate (Senate Banking Committee markup; Senate Legislative Calendar No. 423) / House Agriculture digital-assets subcommittee (Rep. Dusty Johnson statement)
items.title: CLARITY Act placed on Senate Legislative Calendar No. 423; House Agriculture chair commits to fast follow; August recess is the operative deadline; seven Democratic votes remain the gap to cloture
items.facts: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act has been placed on the U.S. Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 423, eligible for a floor vote at any time Senate leadership chooses to schedule one, following a 15-9 Senate Banking Committee markup on May 14, 2026. As reported by The Defiant on June 19, 2026, House Agriculture digital-assets subcommittee chair Rep. Dusty Johnson stated on June 18 that the House will move immediately on a companion measure if the Senate passes the bill before the August recess, removing the need for a conference committee. The bill requires approximately 60 votes to clear a Senate filibuster — about seven Democratic votes beyond full Republican unity. Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.) has cited July 4 as a target; Sen. Cynthia Lummis has said August recess is more realistic; Galaxy Research has cut its passage-before-recess probability to 60%. Outstanding obstacles include an ethics-language dispute, stablecoin-yield rules, and a parallel lobbying campaign by gaming, tribal gaming, and labor groups demanding the bill include explicit language barring prediction markets from offering sports event contracts. The bill would assign digital commodities to CFTC spot-market authority, investment-contract assets to the SEC, and stablecoins to banking regulators under the GENIUS Act framework. Failure to pass before the August recess pushes the bill into a fall midterm calendar.
items.source_label: The Defiant (June 19, 2026; reporting CLARITY Act Senate Calendar No. 423 placement, Rep. Johnson House fast-follow statement, and 7-Democrat cloture math; corroborated by PYMNTS.com, Yahoo Finance, CoinPedia, and Seeking Alpha)
items.relevant_to: crypto exchanges, digital-asset market participants, stablecoin issuers, prediction-market platforms, brokerages, DeFi protocols, fintech companies

items.issuing_body: American Gaming Association, Indian Gaming Association, AFL-CIO Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, UNITE HERE (coalition letter to U.S. Senate, June 16, 2026)
items.title: AGA, tribal gaming groups, and labor unions send Senate letter demanding CLARITY Act include explicit ban on prediction-market sports event contracts
items.facts: On June 16, 2026, a coalition led by the American Gaming Association (AGA), the Indian Gaming Association, the AFL-CIO's Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, and UNITE HERE sent a letter to the U.S. Senate urging legislators to amend the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act to include explicit language barring prediction markets from offering sports and casino-style event contracts, arguing that sports betting 'falls outside the CFTC's remit and cannot be offered through prediction market platforms.' As reported by The Defiant (and corroborated by CryptoNews, AMBCrypto, Sportsbook Review, Yogonet, BanklessTimes, and Covers.com), the letter states that prediction markets have 'fueled the largest expansion of gambling in U.S. history over the past 18 months, without voter approval or legislative authorization,' and the AGA has separately estimated states have lost roughly $1 billion in gaming tax revenue to prediction markets since the start of 2025. The Senate Banking Committee advanced the CLARITY Act on a 15-9 vote in May 2026; a full Senate floor vote has not yet been scheduled.
items.source_label: The Defiant (June 17, 2026; reporting the AGA/Indian Gaming Association/AFL-CIO/UNITE HERE letter to the Senate; corroborated by CryptoNews, AMBCrypto, Sportsbook Review, Yogonet, BanklessTimes, and Covers.com)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market operators, gaming operators, tribal gaming entities, sportsbooks, CFTC-registered entities

items.issuing_body: Kentucky Office of the Attorney General (Russell Coleman) — Franklin Circuit Court
items.title: Kentucky AG sues Kalshi, Polymarket, and VGW alleging illegal unlicensed gambling operations
items.facts: On June 17, 2026, Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman filed lawsuits in Franklin Circuit Court against prediction-market operators Kalshi and Polymarket and against online sweepstakes-casino operator VGW (operator of Chumba Casino, Global Poker, and LuckyLand Slots), alleging the companies are conducting illegal, unlicensed gambling operations within the Commonwealth. As reported by Covers (and corroborated by Gambling Insider, Gambling News, LEX18, Yogonet, PlayUSA, and LINK nky), the suits allege Kalshi and Polymarket are effectively operating sportsbooks in Kentucky without the licenses required of regulated sports-betting operators and provide inadequate responsible-gambling protections; one complaint names Kalshi and affiliated companies including Coinbase, and the Attorney General stated that Polymarket, Kalshi, and affiliated entities including Coinbase, Robinhood, and Webull offer limited or no tools for users to identify gambling-related problems. The suits seek temporary and permanent injunctive relief and all recoverable damages available to the Commonwealth. The filings came days after the Coalition for Fair Markets (Kalshi, Polymarket US, and Crypto.com's derivatives exchange) sued Kentucky over its newly enacted 14.25% prediction-market tax and related restrictions.
items.source_label: Covers (June 19, 2026; reporting AG Coleman's suits against Kalshi, Polymarket, and VGW; corroborated by Gambling Insider, Gambling News, LEX18, Yogonet, PlayUSA, LINK nky)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market operators, sweepstakes / social-casino operators, sportsbooks, crypto exchanges, payment processors serving these platforms

items.issuing_body: CFTC — U.S. District Court, Northern District of Illinois
items.title: CFTC amends its Illinois lawsuit and seeks a preliminary injunction against the state's new 'exchange wager' prediction-market tax
items.facts: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission amended its lawsuit against the State of Illinois (N.D. Illinois, No. 1:26-cv-03659, originally filed April 2, 2026) after Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker signed a budget creating a new tax structure for prediction markets. As reported by Gambling Insider, the amended complaint challenges Illinois's new 'exchange wager' provisions, arguing the state is attempting to regulate event-contract markets that fall within the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act; the new Illinois law would impose transaction fees ranging from 1.75% to 3.5% on sports event contracts. The CFTC also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction seeking to block Illinois from enforcing its gambling laws against event contracts while the litigation proceeds, arguing the state is engaged in a 'targeted campaign of regulatory hostility' toward prediction markets.
items.source_label: Gambling Insider (June 19, 2026 weekly roundup; reporting the CFTC's amended Illinois complaint and PI motion; corroborated by Bitcoin Foundation news and prior Crain's/CNBC coverage of the underlying April 2026 suit)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market / event-contract platforms, crypto derivatives exchanges, CFTC registrants, tax and compliance teams

items.issuing_body: Matthew Mazza (plaintiff) — U.S. District Court, Northern District of California
items.title: Proposed class action alleges Robinhood runs an unlicensed sports-gambling operation through its prediction-markets hub
items.facts: On June 10, 2026, a proposed class action (Mazza v. Robinhood) was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against Robinhood Markets, Inc. and its subsidiary Robinhood Derivatives, alleging the company operates an unlicensed, illegal sports-gambling operation marketed as an investment product through its 'prediction markets hub.' As reported by Casino.org (and corroborated by Bloomberg Law, Sportsbook Review, Gambling News, and CDC Gaming), the complaint alleges Robinhood's sports event contracts are effectively sports wagers rather than financial products, that the platform let customers bet against margin using existing stock holdings (allowing wagers with borrowed money and losses exceeding deposits) without clearly disclosing the risk at the point of trade, and that Robinhood created a misleading impression the products had state regulatory approval. The named plaintiff alleges he lost approximately $400,000 in fees, commissions, and wagers in 2025-2026. Robinhood began offering sports event contracts through a partnership with Kalshi in March 2025. The suit seeks to recover alleged customer losses.
items.source_label: Casino.org (reporting the N.D. Cal. Mazza v. Robinhood class action; corroborated by Bloomberg Law, Sportsbook Review, Gambling News, CDC Gaming)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market operators, brokerages offering event contracts, fintech platforms, consumer-protection and compliance teams

items.issuing_body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
items.title: Sixth Circuit consolidates the Ohio (Kalshi v. Schuler) and Tennessee prediction-market appeals
items.facts: As reported by Gambling Insider, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit consolidated Kalshi's Ohio appeal (KalshiEx LLC v. Schuler, No. 26-3196) with a related Tennessee appeal, uniting two cases that produced conflicting lower-court rulings on whether states can regulate sports event contracts offered on federally regulated exchanges. The consolidation was reported in the same period in which the court denied the CFTC's motion to participate as an amicus at oral argument in the Ohio appeal.
items.source_label: Gambling Insider (June 19, 2026 weekly roundup; reporting the Sixth Circuit's consolidation of the Ohio and Tennessee appeals)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market operators, event-contract platforms, CFTC registrants, sportsbooks

items.issuing_body: Cayuga Nation (plaintiff) — U.S. District Court, Northern District of New York
items.title: Cayuga Nation sues Caesars Sportsbook over mobile bets placed on tribal land — first tribal lawsuit against licensed sportsbook; novel IGRA 'where is the bet placed' geolocation theory
items.facts: On June 16, 2026, the Cayuga Nation of New York filed a federal lawsuit in the Northern District of New York against American Wagering, Inc. (d/b/a Caesars Sportsbook), alleging that Caesars accepted mobile sports wagers from people physically located on the Cayuga reservation between January 8, 2022 and July 15, 2025, without tribal authorization, a gaming compact, or federal oversight. The complaint alleges violations of the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA): it argues that a mobile sports wager is placed at the bettor's physical location, not at the operator's server, and therefore betting accepted from within the reservation constitutes Class III gaming on Indian lands, requiring a tribal gaming ordinance and a federally approved tribal-state compact that the Cayuga Nation does not have for sports betting. The Nation sent Caesars a cease-and-desist letter on June 20, 2025; Caesars subsequently agreed to geofence the reservation but declined to provide a full accounting of prior revenue. The complaint seeks damages, an accounting of reservation-bet revenue, and a declaration that Caesars' mobile operations on Cayuga lands were unauthorized. Gaming attorney Daniel Wallach identified this as the first known case of a tribe suing a state-licensed sportsbook over online bets placed from Indian lands. The Cayuga Nation operates Class II gaming venues (LakeSide Entertainment) in New York's Finger Lakes region.
items.source_label: Casino.org (Philip Conneller, published June 18, 2026; confirmed by fingerlakes1.com, SBC Americas, BettorsInsider, CasinoBeats, CDC Gaming, iGamingToday)
items.relevant_to: licensed mobile sportsbook operators, payment processors handling mobile betting, geolocation and compliance technology vendors, tribal gaming operators

items.issuing_body: U.S. Senate
items.title: U.S. Senate passes 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644) with statutory Fed CBDC ban through 2030; House concurrence vote pending
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, the U.S. Senate invoked cloture (84-8) and passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644). The bill includes a provision banning the Federal Reserve from issuing or creating a central bank digital currency (CBDC) or any substantially similar asset, directly or through an intermediary, through December 31, 2030. The CBDC ban defines a CBDC as a dollar-denominated digital asset that is U.S. currency, a direct liability of the Federal Reserve System, and widely available to the public; it carves out dollar-denominated, open, permissionless, and private digital currencies with privacy protections comparable to physical U.S. currency. Senate passage follows the release of reconciled bill text on June 16, 2026 by Sen. Tim Scott, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Rep. French Hill, and Rep. Maxine Waters, and a Motion to Proceed vote of 87-8 earlier in the day. The amended bill returns to the House for concurrence in the Senate amendment (H.Res.1299 provides the rule for consideration of the concurrence). Prior votes: Senate 89-10 in March (prior version); House 396-13 in May. Note: this entry supplements the June 18 entry (2026-06-18-congress-cbdc-ban-road-to-housing-act) covering the bill text release.
items.source_label: U.S. Senate Daily Press (June 18, 2026; floor votes including 84-8 cloture; corroborated by NACo 'Senate Passes 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act' and Latham Watkins analysis)
items.relevant_to: stablecoin issuers, payment and fintech platforms, banks, digital-dollar infrastructure providers

items.issuing_body: U.S. District Court, W.D. Michigan (Judge Paul Maloney)
items.title: W.D. Michigan denies Robinhood preliminary injunction — sports event contracts are NOT swaps; CEA does not clearly preempt state gambling law
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, U.S. District Judge Paul Maloney of the Western District of Michigan denied Robinhood's motion for a preliminary injunction against Michigan state gambling enforcement in a second, near-identical ruling to the Polymarket denial issued the same day. The court held on two independent grounds: (1) sports event contracts of the type Robinhood offers are not 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act, placing them outside the CFTC's exclusive swap jurisdiction; and (2) even if the contracts were swaps, it is not clearly established that the CEA would preempt Michigan's state gambling law in this context. The Gambling Insider article reports the two opinions are 'nearly identical' and contains direct quotes from both. Together, the Polymarket and Robinhood W.D. Michigan rulings are the first federal court holdings that sports event contracts fall outside the CEA swap definition and that CEA preemption of state gambling law is not clearly established — both holdings run contrary to the CFTC's preemption position. Both cases continue on the merits. See also: 2026-06-17-polymarket-michigan-pi-denied.
items.source_label: Gambling Insider (June 18, 2026; covers both Polymarket and Robinhood opinions; direct quotes from rulings; corroborated by Decrypt)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market operators, event-contract platforms, brokerages offering sports contracts, state gaming regulators

items.issuing_body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
items.title: Sixth Circuit denies CFTC motion to participate as amicus at oral argument in KalshiEx v. Schuler (No. 26-3196)
items.facts: On June 16, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit denied the CFTC's motion to appear as an amicus curiae at oral argument in KalshiEx LLC v. Matthew T. Schuler et al. (No. 26-3196), Kalshi's appeal of a lower court denial of its preliminary injunction against Ohio state enforcement. The CFTC had submitted a written amicus brief on May 12, 2026, asserting exclusive CFTC jurisdiction over prediction markets and arguing for CEA preemption of state gambling laws. The court's denial is a procedural ruling that does not resolve the merits of CFTC jurisdiction or CEA preemption, but it limits the CFTC's ability to advocate its preemption position directly before the panel at oral argument. Oral argument in KalshiEx v. Schuler proceeds without live CFTC participation.
items.source_label: SBC Americas (June 17, 2026; covers states and tribes court mobilization against prediction markets, including 6th Circuit context); confirmed by Law360 ('6th Circ. Says CFTC Can't Argue In Kalshi, Ohio Betting Fight', subscription required)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market operators, event-contract platforms, CFTC-registered entities

items.issuing_body: Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC, NCUA, and Treasury (FinCEN)
items.title: Five federal agencies propose a customer identification program rule for payment stablecoin issuers (GENIUS Act)
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board — jointly with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) — requested comment on a proposed rule that would require certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) to maintain an effective customer identification program (CIP), with requirements comparable to the customer identification program requirements for banks and credit unions, implementing the GENIUS Act. According to the proposal, the program must include reasonable procedures for verifying the identity of any person seeking to open an account to the extent reasonable and practicable; maintaining records of the information used to verify a person's identity, including name, address, and other identifying information; and determining whether the person appears on any government-provided lists of known or suspected terrorists or terrorist organizations. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. The agencies' 130-page proposal also asks whether any CIP requirement should be extended to secondary market activity; Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr issued a statement saying the GENIUS Act framework 'does not do enough so far to address the risks of illicit finance conducted through secondary market transactions in payment stablecoins.'
items.source_label: Federal Reserve Board Press Release (June 18, 2026); joint with OCC, FDIC, NCUA, and Treasury/FinCEN. Federal Register notice and Gov. Barr statement linked from the release.
items.relevant_to: payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs), crypto exchanges and custodians, banks and credit unions entering stablecoins, BSA/AML and compliance teams

items.issuing_body: State of Illinois (Gov. JB Pritzker)
items.title: Illinois enacts first-in-nation digital-asset transaction tax (SB 3019 / Digital Asset Tax Act)
items.facts: Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed Senate Bill 3019, the Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA), as part of the state's $55.9 billion budget, making Illinois the first U.S. state to impose a transaction-based tax on digital-asset activity. The law imposes a 0.2% privilege tax on brokers who exchange, transfer, or store digital assets for customers in the state; it applies to brokers with a physical presence in Illinois or an economic nexus (more than $100,000 in gross receipts from Illinois customers), takes effect January 1, 2027, and is projected to generate roughly $60 million. The Crypto Council for Innovation has requested a line-item veto of the article establishing the levy, and The Digital Chamber and the Illinois Blockchain Association issued a joint letter opposing the measure; critics note no comparable state transaction tax applies to stocks, bonds, or derivatives.
items.source_label: Crypto Briefing (reporting Illinois SB 3019 / Digital Asset Tax Act; signing also reported by Yahoo Finance, Bitcoin Magazine, The Defiant, and others)
items.relevant_to: crypto exchanges, brokers, custodians and wallet providers with Illinois nexus; payment processors; tax/compliance teams

items.issuing_body: U.S. Senate Banking Committee (Congress)
items.title: Congress folds a statutory Fed CBDC ban (through 2030) into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644)
items.facts: On June 16, 2026, the leaders of the Senate Banking and House Financial Services Committees — Sen. Tim Scott, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Rep. French Hill, and Rep. Maxine Waters — released updated bill text for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (H.R. 6644), a combined Senate, House, and White House package. According to the release and reporting on the text, the package folds in a statutory ban on a Federal Reserve central bank digital currency (CBDC): it amends the Federal Reserve Act to provide that the Fed 'may not issue or create' a CBDC or any substantially similar asset, directly or through an intermediary, through December 31, 2030; defines a CBDC as a dollar-denominated digital asset that is U.S. currency, a direct liability of the Federal Reserve System, and widely available to the public; and carves out a dollar-denominated, open, permissionless, and private digital currency with privacy protections comparable to physical U.S. currency. The reconciled text returns to the Senate floor for final action; a prior version passed the Senate 89-10 in March and the House passed its amended version 396-13 in May. See also: 2026-06-19-senate-passes-road-housing-cbdc-ban for Senate passage update.
items.source_label: U.S. Senate Banking Committee Press Release (June 16, 2026)
items.relevant_to: stablecoin issuers, payment and fintech platforms, banks, digital-dollar infrastructure providers

items.issuing_body: Tribal Amici (coalition of federally recognized tribes)
items.title: Tribal coalition files amicus briefs opposing CFTC/Kalshi preemption of tribal gaming laws
items.facts: A coalition of federally recognized tribes and tribal regulatory bodies, calling itself the Tribal Amici, filed amicus briefs this month in two federal prediction-market cases, arguing that allowing Kalshi and the CFTC to override state gaming laws would also nullify tribal-state gaming compacts and strip tribes of authority to regulate prediction markets on Native land. The coalition filed a brief opposing Kalshi's preliminary-injunction motion in KalshiEx LLC v. Schuler, now before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, and a separate filing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York backing the state's opposition to the CFTC's preliminary-injunction motion. In both briefs the coalition contends that a ruling for Kalshi or the CFTC would be a 'sub silentio reversal of congressional policy and Supreme Court precedent' and would 'undermine existing tribal-state gaming compacts and regulatory frameworks' negotiated under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.
items.source_label: The Defiant (reporting the Tribal Amici amicus briefs; links the CourtListener docket and the S.D.N.Y. filing; corroborated by Protos)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market / event-contract platforms, tribal gaming operators, sportsbooks, exchanges

items.issuing_body: CFTC
items.title: CFTC enters final consent order against Celsius Network and CEO Mashinsky — civil fraud, CEL token manipulation, and unregistered pool charges resolved; DOJ criminal case continues
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, the CFTC entered a final consent order against Celsius Network LLC and its former CEO Alex Mashinsky resolving civil enforcement claims arising from the 2022 collapse of the Celsius crypto-lending platform. The consent order resolves three enforcement theories: (1) fraudulent misrepresentation of deposit safety and liquidity practices to retail customers — Celsius represented to depositors that their assets were safe and liquid when, in fact, the platform faced material undisclosed risks; (2) market manipulation through coordinated trading in Celsius's native CEL token, which the CFTC classified as a commodity; and (3) operating as an unregistered commodity pool operator (CPO) without CFTC registration, in violation of the CEA. The consent order resolves the CFTC's civil enforcement action; the U.S. Department of Justice's separate criminal case against Mashinsky continues. Celsius Network ceased operations in 2022 and remains in bankruptcy proceedings.
items.source_label: CFTC Press Release 9256-26
items.relevant_to: crypto lending platforms, token issuers, crypto exchanges, platform executives

items.issuing_body: CFTC and SEC
items.title: CFTC and SEC issue joint Request for Information on event contracts and prediction markets (Release 9258-26)
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, the CFTC and SEC jointly issued Release 9258-26, a Request for Information on event-based contracts and the application of existing regulatory frameworks to prediction markets. The RFI asks market participants and the public to comment on questions including: when event contracts constitute swaps subject to CFTC jurisdiction, futures subject to CFTC jurisdiction, or securities subject to SEC jurisdiction; how existing statutory definitions should apply to contracts on sports, political, and other event outcomes; and whether the current dual-agency framework requires clarification or new rulemaking. This is the first joint inter-agency RFI on the jurisdictional classification of event contracts and prediction markets. The comment deadline has not yet been announced; it will appear in the Federal Register.
items.source_label: CFTC Press Release 9258-26
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, event-contract operators, crypto exchanges, derivatives platforms

items.issuing_body: CFTC and SEC
items.title: CFTC and SEC issue joint Request for Information on derivatives data reporting modernization (Release 9257-26)
items.facts: On June 18, 2026, the CFTC and SEC jointly issued Release 9257-26, a Request for Information on derivatives data reporting and regulatory technology modernization. The RFI covers three topic areas: (1) swap data repository (SDR) reporting obligations and the data standards applicable to reportable transactions; (2) real-time public reporting of swap transaction data; and (3) the potential for new data-field standards and data-exchange formats to improve regulatory oversight and reduce compliance costs for registrants. The RFI is a companion to the joint event-contracts RFI (Release 9258-26) issued the same day. The comment deadline has not yet been announced; it will appear in the Federal Register.
items.source_label: CFTC Press Release 9257-26
items.relevant_to: derivatives market participants, swap data repositories, crypto derivatives platforms, CFTC registrants

items.issuing_body: CME Group — U.S. District Court
items.title: CME Group sues CFTC over approval of perpetual bitcoin futures (BTCPERP) on Kalshi — argues perps are swaps not futures; challenges 24-hour self-certification as APA violation
items.facts: CME Group filed suit against the CFTC challenging the agency's June 2026 approval of 24/7 perpetual bitcoin futures contracts (BTCPERP) on KalshiEx via the CFTC's Regulation 40.2 self-certification process. CME's complaint presents two principal arguments: (1) that perpetual futures contracts — which have no fixed expiration date and settle continuously — are 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act rather than futures, and that the CFTC therefore lacked authority to approve them for trading as futures on a designated contract market; and (2) that using the 24-hour self-certification process rather than the agency's full rule-review process for a novel product of this type violated the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements. Coinbase and Kalshi had announced a planned launch of BTCPERP; that launch faces injunction risk while the litigation proceeds.
items.source_label: Markets Media (reporting the CME Group v. CFTC lawsuit)
items.relevant_to: crypto derivatives platforms, perpetual futures operators, Kalshi, Coinbase, CFTC registrants

items.issuing_body: U.S. District Court, W.D. Michigan
items.title: W.D. Michigan denies Polymarket PI — court rules sports event contracts are NOT 'swaps' under the CEA; CEA may not preempt state gambling law even if they were
items.facts: On June 17, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan denied Polymarket's motion for a preliminary injunction against enforcement of Michigan state gambling law. The court rested its denial on two independent holdings: (1) sports event contracts of the type Polymarket offers are not 'swaps' under the Commodity Exchange Act, meaning the CFTC's exclusive swap jurisdiction does not cover them; and (2) even if the contracts were classified as swaps, it is not clearly established that the CEA would preempt Michigan's state gambling law in this context. The case continues on the merits. The ruling is the first federal court holding that sports event contracts fall outside the CEA swap definition and that CEA preemption of state gambling law is not clearly established — two holdings directly contrary to the CFTC's preemption position. See also: 2026-06-19-robinhood-michigan-pi-denied (same court, same judge, near-identical opinion issued June 18).
items.source_label: SBC Americas (reporting the W.D. Michigan PI denial)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, event-contract operators, state gaming regulators, sportsbooks

items.issuing_body: NYDFS
items.title: NYDFS proposes stablecoin regulation aligning New York's framework with the federal GENIUS Act
items.facts: On June 9, 2026, the New York State Department of Financial Services, under Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow, proposed a regulation to build on New York's existing stablecoin framework and align it with the federal GENIUS Act. The proposal carries forward DFS's prior requirements for U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins issued under its oversight — backing and redeemability, permissible reserves, and independent audits — and adds new federal provisions, including setting maximum amounts of reserves that can be held at any one custodian and requiring issuers to adopt risk-management programs covering internal controls, information security, internal audit, asset growth, earnings, insider and affiliate transactions, and service-provider arrangements. The proposed regulation is subject to a 10-day preproposal comment period beginning June 9, 2026, followed by a 60-day comment period upon publication in the State Register; the final regulation would take effect at the same time as the GENIUS Act becomes effective, with a one-year transition period for existing New York-licensed issuers. The Department's June 2022 stablecoin guidance remains in effect until then.
items.source_label: NYDFS Press Release (June 9, 2026)
items.relevant_to: stablecoin issuers, virtual-currency (BitLicense) licensees, custodians, payment-stablecoin platforms

items.issuing_body: CFTC
items.title: CFTC issues Request for Information on fintech innovation, AI, and digital asset technologies (Release 9254-26)
items.facts: On June 16, 2026, the CFTC issued Release 9254-26, a Request for Information on fintech innovation, artificial intelligence, and digital asset technologies. The RFI covers five topic areas: (1) decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and their interaction with CFTC-regulated markets, including whether DeFi participants may be acting as unregistered intermediaries; (2) artificial intelligence and machine learning applications in trading, risk management, and regulatory compliance, including automated order routing and AI-generated trading strategies; (3) real-world asset (RWA) tokenization and its implications for CFTC-regulated derivatives markets; (4) payment stablecoins and their use as margin, collateral, or settlement assets in derivatives transactions; and (5) cybersecurity and operational resilience for digital-asset market participants. The comment window is currently open; the deadline will appear in the Federal Register. Note: this item is backfilled from June 16 — the publication date precedes the date the item entered this intake batch.
items.source_label: CFTC Press Release 9254-26
items.relevant_to: DeFi protocols, crypto exchanges, stablecoin issuers, AI trading firms, RWA tokenization platforms

items.issuing_body: Pennsylvania Supreme Court
items.title: Pennsylvania Supreme Court rules skill games are slot machines; 120-day enforcement stay issued
items.facts: On June 15, 2026, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court issued its majority opinion in J-97-2025 (Pace-O-Matic v. Pennsylvania), ruling that skill game machines 'are subject to both the Gaming Act and the Crimes Code,' overturning a Commonwealth Court ruling the Justices called 'deeply flawed.' Justice David Wecht wrote that the POM device is 'several times over' a slot machine and the legal definition 'describes the POM device with precision.' The Court issued a 120-day enforcement stay during which law enforcement cannot take action against owners and operators, and noted the General Assembly 'remains free at any time to take whatever legislative action it may deem appropriate.' Pace-O-Matic stated it is 'disappointed,' said the impact on 10,000+ small businesses and fraternal clubs presents an 'impossible choice,' and will pursue a legislative solution; bipartisan bills SB 1079 (Sen. Yaw) and HB 2213 (Rep. Burgos) are cited. Pennsylvania AG Dave Sunday called the ruling 'a significant victory for consumers, taxpayers, and the rule of law.' An estimated 70,000+ skill game machines operate in bars, VFWs, restaurants, and fraternal clubs statewide.
items.source_label: Pennsylvania Supreme Court Opinion J-97-2025 (majority opinion)
items.relevant_to: skill game operators, gaming venues (bars, VFWs, fraternal clubs), payment processors, PA legislators

items.issuing_body: State of Wisconsin (Attorney General) — U.S. District Court, W.D. Wis.
items.title: Wisconsin moves to block sports event-contract trading on Coinbase, Kalshi, and Robinhood
items.facts: As reported by DeFi Rate (and corroborated by Gambling Insider and Bettors Insider), on 2026-06-09 the State of Wisconsin filed a motion for a preliminary injunction in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin seeking to block KalshiEX, Coinbase, and Robinhood from offering sports event-contract trading to people in the state until the court rules on the merits of its underlying lawsuit (State of Wisconsin v. Kalshi et al., filed April 2026). The brief characterizes the trading as 'open, repeated, ongoing criminal violations' of state law and a public-nuisance violation, argues the state's residents suffer irreparable harm from unregulated gambling, and contends the Commodity Exchange Act does not preempt Wisconsin's sports-wagering laws. The defendants have not yet responded.
items.source_label: DeFi Rate (reporting the Wisconsin preliminary-injunction motion)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, crypto exchanges, brokerages

items.issuing_body: Gary Gensler (amicus) — U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
items.title: Gensler files Sixth Circuit amicus arguing sports prediction markets are not 'swaps'
items.facts: As reported by The Defiant (and corroborated by DeFi Rate), on 2026-06-11 former CFTC and SEC chair Gary Gensler filed an amicus brief with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit in KalshiEX LLC v. Schuler — Kalshi's appeal of an Ohio district court's denial of a preliminary injunction — arguing that sports-event prediction-market contracts fall outside the statutory definition of a 'swap' under Dodd-Frank and are therefore not within the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction. The brief contends the swap definition centers on hedging economic risk and that reading it to cover sports bets would imply every off-exchange wager since October 2012 had been illegal. The position contradicts the CFTC's own May 12, 2026 amicus asserting exclusive jurisdiction.
items.source_label: The Defiant (reporting the Gensler Sixth Circuit amicus brief)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, derivatives exchanges, crypto exchanges

items.issuing_body: Delaware General Assembly (HB 441) / New Jersey Legislature (S-2141)
items.title: Delaware (HB 441) and New Jersey (S-2141) advance statewide crypto-ATM bans
items.facts: As reported by The Defiant (and corroborated by Cointelegraph, CryptoNews, and Grafa), Delaware and New Jersey have each advanced legislation to ban cryptocurrency ATMs statewide, citing fraud losses. Delaware's House Bill 441 cleared the House Economic Development Committee and passed the House; it would require existing kiosks to go dark upon enactment and be physically removed within 90 days, bar cashier-assisted workarounds, and expose operators to unlawful-trade-practice charges plus victim-refund and forfeiture obligations. New Jersey's Senate Bill S-2141 cleared the Senate Commerce Committee unanimously and heads to the full chamber. Sponsors cited FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center data of 13,400 crypto-ATM-scam complaints in 2025 and more than $388 million in losses (a 58% year-over-year increase), with more than half of complaints involving victims over 60; operator CoinFlip urged regulation with transaction monitoring instead of prohibition. Tennessee, Indiana, and Minnesota already have statewide bans.
items.source_label: The Defiant (reporting the Delaware and New Jersey crypto-ATM ban bills)
items.relevant_to: crypto-ATM/kiosk operators, payment processors, compliance vendors

items.issuing_body: Financial Technology Association v. Tennessee — Davidson County Chancery Court
items.title: Fintech trade group sues Tennessee to block remittance tax (HB2502)
items.facts: As reported by The Center Square (and corroborated by Law360, CU Today, and Fintech Business Weekly), the Financial Technology Association filed suit in Davidson County (Tennessee) Chancery Court seeking an injunction to block HB2502, a law signed by Gov. Bill Lee in May 2026 that adds a $10 fee on monetary wire transfers to another country plus a 2% tax on transfers over $500 (effective Jan. 1, 2027; projected to raise more than $91 million in FY2026-27). The FTA argues the law is unconstitutional under the dormant Commerce Clause because it singles out international payments for special taxation, and its complaint states members will have to modify transaction-processing systems, compliance software, and customer-facing interfaces, incurring nonrecoverable compliance costs before year-end or risk penalties. FTA president and CEO Penny Lee said, 'when a state singles out international payments for special taxation, that is unconstitutional, plain and simple.'
items.source_label: The Center Square (reporting the FTA v. Tennessee filing)
items.relevant_to: money transmitters, remittance providers, payment processors, fintechs

items.issuing_body: CFTC
items.title: CFTC sues New Mexico over prediction-market preemption (8th state)
items.facts: On 2026-06-12 the CFTC filed suit in federal court against the State of New Mexico, seeking a declaratory judgment that federal law grants it exclusive authority over event contracts and a permanent injunction barring the state from enforcing preempted gaming laws against CFTC registrants. The action follows New Mexico's state-court suit against CFTC-registrant KalshiEX LLC alleging its prediction-market offerings are unlawful online sports betting. The release states New Mexico joins AZ, CT, IL, NY, MN, RI, and WI.
items.source_label: CFTC Press Release 9251-26
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, sportsbooks, exchanges, CFTC registrants

items.issuing_body: Nevada Gaming Control Board
items.title: Nevada gaming regulator seeks to hold Kalshi in contempt over prediction-market geofencing
items.facts: As reported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal (and corroborated by InterGame and Gambling Insider), on 2026-06-12 the Nevada Gaming Control Board petitioned the First Judicial District Court in Carson City to find KalshiEx LLC in contempt for allegedly not complying with a May 18 order requiring it to geofence its website so it cannot offer sports-, election-, or entertainment-related event contracts to anyone located in Nevada. The Board asked the court to impose sanctions, including disgorgement of profits from Nevada transactions or daily penalties until compliance. A Kalshi spokesperson said the company has complied, attributed the issue to a technology glitch, and called the filing a 'PR stunt.'
items.source_label: Las Vegas Review-Journal (reporting the Nevada GCB court filing)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, geolocation/compliance vendors, sportsbooks

items.issuing_body: Coalition for Fair Markets (NADEX, Kalshi, Polymarket/QCX)
items.title: Prediction-market coalition sues Kentucky over 14.25% tax on event-contract trading
items.facts: As reported by SBC Americas (first reported by the Associated Press and corroborated by Gambling Insider), on 2026-06-12 the Coalition for Fair Markets — comprising Crypto.com's North American Derivatives Exchange (NADEX), Kalshi, and Polymarket's U.S. exchange QCX — filed suit in Franklin Circuit Court to block Kentucky from implementing a 14.25% tax on prediction-market transaction fees set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027, arguing the measure unlawfully targets federally regulated event-contract exchanges and is preempted by federal derivatives law. The enacted package (HB 757 and HB 904) also bars state-licensed gaming operators from doing business with platforms offering sports event-contract trading in Kentucky, a prohibition due to take effect next month. Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman, a named defendant, said his office 'will defend these statutes.'
items.source_label: SBC Americas (reporting the Coalition for Fair Markets filing; first reported by the Associated Press)
items.relevant_to: prediction-market platforms, licensed gaming operators, payment processors
